item.title: Youth group catches muggers, wears uniforms, conducts raids
item.description:
A video circulating on Facebook shows several young men detaining a man who identifies himself as Anwar, also known as ‘Blade Anwar’.

The young men ask Anwar to send a message to muggers operating in Tongi. Anwar then says, “Don’t come to Tongi to carry out mugging. They will beat you and break your bones.”

At this point, someone off camera asks, “Who will break their bones?” Anwar replies, “The public.”

The young men then ask Anwar to say the name of an organisation called Bangladesh Youth Revolution. He tries to say the name and the video ends there.

The incident took place on 16 August in Tongi, Gazipur. The organisation mentioned in the video was formed by a group of young people from the Tongi area.

Bangladesh Youth Revolution’s central convener Fahad Islam is a third-year undergraduate student at Tongi Government College. He told Prothom Alo that they mainly work against people involved in crimes such as mugging and drug use. They catch people involved in such activities red-handed and hand them over to the police.

Fahad Islam said 250 members are currently working with the group in the Tongi area. Another 700 or so CVs have been submitted by people interested in becoming members.

The Bangladesh Youth Revolution Facebook page has 54,000 followers. The group regularly posts videos of people they claim are muggers, drug users and drug dealers after detaining them. These videos gain thousands of views. Group members patrol the area and take part in operations wearing designated uniforms. They have also been seen in their uniforms alongside police officers. They carry sticks and other makeshift weapons. At times, people suspected of mugging are beaten and subjected to humiliating punishment.

250 members are currently working with the group in the Tongi area. Another 700 or so CVs have been submitted by people interested in becoming members.

Questions have nevertheless been raised about why young people should be doing the work of the police. Some point out that it is risky to leave the task of apprehending criminals in the hands of ordinary citizens. Who can guarantee that no member of the group will harass an innocent person or use the group to serve personal interests? Identifying a suspect as a criminal and circulating a video of them can also constitute an offence.

Muggings in Tongi

The Tongi area of Gazipur falls under two police stations, Tongi East and Tongi West. According to Google, the two police stations are about four kilometres apart. Local residents allege that despite police from two stations working in the same area, they have failed to effectively control crime.

According to Tongi East police, 71 cases were filed over mugging, attempted mugging and robbery between June and September last year. During the period, 702 alleged muggers were detained. At Tongi West police station, 72 cases were filed over mugging and attempted robbery during the same period and 425 people were detained.

The Bangladesh Youth Revolution Facebook page has 54,000 followers. The group regularly posts videos of people they claim are muggers, drug users and drug dealers after detaining them. These videos gain thousands of views.

However, these figures do not provide a complete picture of crime in the area. Victims often do not file cases after being mugged. In many instances, police also record complaints as general diaries (GDs) instead of filing cases.

Officer-in-charge (OC) of Tongi East police station Maksudul Alam told Prothom Alo that mugging and drug dealing among other crimes have declined and regular drives remain ongoing.

Nevertheless, visiting different parts of Tongi on 26-27 September and speaking with local residents and police personnel revealed that muggers remain active across several spots, including Station Road, Hossain Market, College Gate, Abdullahpur bus stand, Sataish, Keranirtek and the Haji Mazar slum. Muggings occur frequently in these areas, particularly in the evening and at night.

Sabuj Uddin, Chief Organiser, Bangladesh Youth RevolutionWe do this to ensure the safety of our mothers and sisters.

On 26 August at around 3:30am, Sheikh Mohammad Russel, a resident of Sataish, and his family were victims of a mugging in the Tongi area.

Russel told Prothom Alo, “After learning about my aunt’s death, I left home that night with my wife and brother to travel to Rangpur. While we were waiting by the road to board a bus, three men with their faces covered in cloth held sharp weapons to us and robbed two mobile phones, gold ornaments and cash.”

The following day, Russel filed a case with Tongi West police station. He told Prothom Alo, “None of the stolen items have been recovered, nor have I received any updates regarding the arrest of the perpetrators.”

Muggers in Tongi remain active across several spots, including Station Road, Hossain Market, College Gate, Abdullahpur bus stand, Sataish, Keranirtek and the Haji Mazar slum. Muggings occur frequently in these areas, particularly in the evening and at night.

The youth group

The group of young people known as Bangladesh Youth Revolution is now familiar to residents of Tongi. The organisers said it was launched on 16 December 2025. Since then, they have detained around 250 alleged muggers and drug dealers and handed them over to the police.

Bangladesh Youth Revolution’s central chief organiser, Sabuj Uddin Iqbal, told Prothom Alo, “When our sources give us information about a crime, we immediately conduct an operation. The police also inform us, saying that crime has increased in a particular area and asking us to patrol there.”

Asked why they carry out such operations when apprehending criminals is the police’s responsibility, Sabuj Uddin said, “We do this to ensure the safety of our mothers and sisters.”

Sabuj Uddin claimed that Bangladesh Youth Revolution members have a WhatsApp group that also includes several officers of the Gazipur Metropolitan Police.

Gazipur Metropolitan Police (GMP) South Division Deputy Commissioner SM Shafiqul Islam told Prothom Alo that maintaining law and order is the responsibility of the police. However, public assistance is necessary. He said it was difficult to maintain law and order without public awareness and cooperation. The police regularly conduct drives, he added.

Omar Faruk, Professor, Department of Criminology and Police Science, Mawlana Bhashani Science and Technology University,Suppose a member of the youth group asks someone for extortion money. If that person refuses, the group member beats him, labels him a drug dealer and hands him over to the police. Would that be acceptable?

Is this acceptable?

Crimes such as mugging, theft, robbery and drug dealing occur across the country. This raises the question of whether it would be acceptable if similar groups were formed across the country.

Omar Faruk, a professor at the Department of Criminology and Police Science at Mawlana Bhashani Science and Technology University, told Prothom Alo that forming groups through private initiatives to combat crime is not acceptable. Such efforts could lead to various forms of crime, he said.

He said, suppose a member of the youth group asks someone for money. If that person refuses, the group member beats him, labels him a drug dealer and hands him over to the police. Would that be acceptable?

item.title: DP World to sign agreement today after lengthy process
item.description:
The leasing process for Chittagong Port’s New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT), which began during the Awami League government, gained momentum under the interim government. As part of that process, DP World, a UAE (United Arab Emirates)-based port operator, is now set to sign an agreement with the elected BNP (BAngladesh Nationalist Party) government.

The agreement is scheduled to be signed at 3:00 pm today, Thursday, at the Investment Bangladesh auditorium. Under the agreement, DP World will operate the terminal for 15 years and collect fees from users.

In return, the company will pay the port authority a one-off fee and a charge for each container. However, the government has not yet disclosed any details of the agreement.

If the agreement is signed, NCT will become the third container terminal at Chittagong Port to be handed over to a foreign operator.

Earlier, during the Awami League government, Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Gateway Terminal (RSGT) received the responsibility of operating the Patenga Container Terminal, which the government had constructed.

During the interim government, APM Terminals, a subsidiary of Denmark-based company Moller–Maersk, received the contract to construct and operate a container terminal at Laldia. During the same period, the government leased the Pangaon Inland Container Terminal in Keraniganj to Switzerland-based Medlog.

Apart from the terminals handed over to foreign operators, Chittagong Port has two other terminals that domestic operators still manage.

Completed in 2007, the nearly one-kilometre-long New Mooring Terminal can accommodate four seagoing vessels and one smaller container vessel simultaneously.

After construction, the terminal initially began operations partially before becoming fully operational. Domestic operators have managed it under short-term contracts. The terminal mainly handles the loading of export containers onto vessels and the unloading of import containers from vessels.

Lengthy leasing process

In 2008, the authorities took an initiative to appoint a foreign operator for the terminal through a competitive tender. They initially shortlisted four of the world’s leading port operators. The list included UK-based P&O, which DP World had acquired. The Awami League government later cancelled the appointment process.

The Awami League government subsequently restarted the process of leasing the terminal. On 17 February 2019, the parties signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) in Abu Dhabi. The agreement was signed between the Government of Dubai and Bangladesh’s Public-Private Partnership Authority (PPP Authority).

On 3 April 2023, the formal process to lease the NCT moved forward after the then prime minister approved the proposal.

Following the fall of the Awami League government in the mass uprising, the interim government assumed office. During its tenure, the leasing process gained momentum.

Before the government’s term ended, the authorities evaluated the technical and financial proposals. They then began negotiations, which continued from 27 January to 2 February this year. Although the interim government advanced preparations for the agreement, a workers’ movement began at the port during this period.

At a press conference on 8 February, Ashik Chowdhury, chief executive officer of the Public-Private Partnership Authority (PPP Authority), said DP World had sought additional time to review the draft agreement.

The government had only two working days left in its term. As a result, the agreement could not be signed within that period.

After the BNP government took office in February, the suspended leasing process began moving forward again. Following a meeting of the joint platform of the two parties on 8 April, DP World submitted a fresh proposal.

After evaluating the technical and financial aspects of the proposal, the parties concluded the negotiations. On 1 October, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs gave in-principle approval to the draft concession agreement to operate the terminal through a foreign operator for 15 years.

During the interim government’s tenure, a movement against leasing the NCT began under the banner of the Port Workers’ Party, creating a deadlock at the port.

At the time, protesters demanded that the authorities make a decision on the matter under an elected government. Now, under the elected government, workers and employees have again become vocal against the lease under the banner of the Port Protection Movement.

At a sit-in programme on Monday, leaders of the Port Protection Movement warned that they would shut down operations at Chittagong Port on Thursday unless the initiative to lease the NCT was cancelled. As part of the movement, protesters held a torch procession in the port area yesterday, Wednesday.

How much will the port change?

Last financial year, the New Mooring Terminal handled around 1.385 million units of containers. This accounted for approximately 44 per cent of the port’s total container traffic. There has been considerable discussion and criticism over how much container traffic will increase if DP World takes charge.

Although DP World ranks among the world’s top 10 port operators, former Chittagong Port Authority board member Zafar Alam believes the company will need to make fresh infrastructure investments to increase the NCT’s capacity.

Speaking to Prothom Alo, he said, “DP World proposed investing US$1 billion in infrastructure a long time ago. To reap the benefits of the NCT, DP World will now need to invest in infrastructure not only at the terminal but also along the routes used to transport containers to and from the port.”

“For this, it is necessary to invest in the proposed Dhirashram Inland Container Depot (ICD) near the production zones and in rail connectivity to the depot. This will improve DP World’s operational efficiency and also benefit import-export trade,” he added.

item.title: Nana Patekar dies at 75: A look back at the legendary actor’s illustrious career
item.description:
ANI_20241009236

What would Indian cinema look like without the unmistakable voice, intensity and screen presence of Nana Patekar?

Veteran actor Nana Patekar, one of the most respected performers in Hindi and Marathi cinema, passed away on Thursday at the age of 75 after suffering a severe cardiac arrest at his residence in Goa.

Patekar was reportedly found unconscious at his home and was rushed to Manipal Hospital in Dona Paula for treatment. He was declared dead at 5:20 am. Physicians tried to revive the actor for around 45 minutes, but he did not respond to the treatment.

Shekhar Salkar, Chief of the Oncology Department at Manipal Hospital, confirmed the actor’s death to news agency ANI and said that a medico-legal case has been registered. A post-mortem examination will also be conducted.

The news marks the end of a long and distinctive acting career that saw Patekar move comfortably between Hindi and Marathi cinema. He was never an actor who needed elaborate introductions. His voice, expressions and ability to bring a certain intensity to even a few lines of dialogue made him instantly recognisable to generations of film audiences.

Born Vishwanath Patekar in Murud-Janjira in Maharashtra’s Raigad district, Nana Patekar studied at Sir J.J. Institute of Applied Art in Mumbai before entering the world of acting. He made his Bollywood acting debut with the 1978 film Gaman and went on to establish himself through a series of challenging roles.

His breakthrough came with films that allowed him to showcase the range that would eventually define his career. His performance in Parinda earned him the National Film Award for Best Supporting Actor, while Krantiveer brought him the National Film Award for Best Actor. He also received acclaim for films such as Agni Sakshi, Khamoshi: The Musical, Ab Tak Chhappan and Apaharan.

For many viewers, however, Patekar was not limited to serious dramas or intense characters. He could be equally effective in commercial cinema and comedy. His performance as Uday Shetty in Welcome introduced him to another generation of viewers and turned the character into one of the most remembered comic roles of his later career.

Patekar’s work also extended beyond acting. He directed Prahaar: The Final Attack and was involved in writing and filmmaking, further reflecting his interest in different aspects of cinema. His career was marked by an ability to move between mainstream films and more performance-driven projects without being easily confined to one particular image.

Over the years, Patekar received several major honours for his contribution to cinema. He won three National Film Awards and four Filmfare Awards, apart from Maharashtra State Film Awards and other recognitions. In 2013, he was conferred the Padma Shri for his contribution to cinema and the arts.

Away from the screen, Patekar’s life also had its share of personal struggles. He married Neelkanti Patekar in 1978. The couple had two sons, Durvasa and Malhar. Their elder son, Durvasa, died at a young age due to illness. Nana and Neelkanti later lived separately for several years due to personal differences, though they remained legally married.

Patekar was also known for his association with social causes and his connection with rural Maharashtra. He remained involved in efforts aimed at supporting farmers and people affected by difficult circumstances, adding another dimension to his public life beyond cinema.

But it was his work as an actor that ultimately left the strongest mark. Whether playing a volatile protagonist, a menacing villain, a police officer or a comic character, Patekar had a way of making his presence felt. He did not rely on conventional glamour. His performances were often built around voice, body language, silences and an intensity that could change the mood of a scene.

His passing leaves behind a body of work that stretches across generations and genres. From Parinda and Krantiveer to Ab Tak Chhappan and Welcome, Nana Patekar created characters that audiences continued to remember long after the films ended.

Indian cinema has lost an actor whose presence was difficult to replicate. Nana Patekar may have been known for many different roles, but his greatest legacy remains the same, an unmistakable performer who brought his own voice, temperament and personality to every character he played.

item.title: Tenzing Norgay’s son says Himalayas sending climate warning
item.description:
As a new biopic puts the life of mountaineer Tenzing Norgay Sherpa on screen, his son says climate change is transforming the Himalayas and making mountaineering increasingly dangerous.

Released on Friday, “Tenzing”, an Apple TV film, recounts the first confirmed ascent to Everest’s summit in 1953.

But it focuses on the journey from the perspective of Tenzing Norgay Sherpa who, together with Edmund Hillary, completed the climb that until then was deemed impossible.

More than seven decades after Sherpa stood atop the world’s highest peak, Nepal is grappling with the aftermath of catastrophic flood that has put a spotlight on the impact of climate change on mountains.

Jamling Tenzing Norgay Sherpa, 61, said that these disasters are “a warning for us”.

“Nepal is very vulnerable to this because half our country is covered with mountains,” he told AFP.

“That’s going to affect the people living lower down below the valley along the river.”

Two years ago, Sherpa saw that his father’s village Thame, at an altitude of 3,800 metres (12,460 feet), was swept away by a devastating flood caused by a glacial lake outburst.

“It’s a big threat. The moment glaciers recede... the lakes are going to rise and then one day, it’s going to breach and break. And that’s exactly what is happening,” he said.

“It happened in Thame, half of the village was wiped off (the map).”

‘Price to pay’

The younger Sherpa followed in his father’s footsteps to Everest in 1996, a dream he had since he was eight years old.

“I looked up to him as my greatest role model, you know, he was my hero, and I wanted to become just like him,” he said.

But the signs of global warming are appearing on Everest itself.

Sherpa said that guides are now finding water appearing at Camp 2 about 6,400 metres (21,000 feet) high.

“There was never water at all. It’s always solid ice up there,” he said.

Sherpa said that comparative photographs of the mountain show how much the glaciers have receded since his father’s climb.

For climbers and mountaineering Sherpa community, the changes are also making their occupation more dangerous, with unpredictable weather and frequent avalanches.

“I think we have to be very careful now as to how we look at mountains and how we approach climbing mountains nowadays,” he said.

Sherpa said that the responsibility of addressing climate change lies largely with the world’s biggest emitters.

“It’s not only affecting us in the Himalayas, it’s affecting European countries, it’s affecting places in the US with all these wildfires,’ he said.

“If we don’t start taking care of our planet, there’s going to be a price to pay.”

‘Long overdue’

The climate-induced disasters affecting mountain communities form a striking backdrop as the film premiers—featuring Genden Phuntsok in the title role, with Tom Hiddleston as Hillary, as well as Willem Dafoe.

Tenzing Norgay Sherpa’s story was long overshadowed in previous accounts told from a Western perspective of the historic trip up the mountain, which measures 8,849 meters (29,032 feet).

“I think it was long overdue, a film, a biopic about my father, his life,” Sherpa said, adding that the pioneer did not get the recognition he deserved.

“But at the same time, he really didn’t care about it. It wasn’t the fame he looked for, why he climbed the mountain. He climbed because it was his passion and he had a dream to climb this mountain,” he said.

Tenzing Norgay Sherpa’s historic climb made the term ‘Sherpa’ synonymous with courageous mountain guides and workers.

Sherpa said that while mountains were a passion for his father and many Nepali climbers are getting recognition, financial necessity still drives the mountaineering industry.

“The Sherpas climb today to keep bread and butter on the table, you know, to feed their children, to give their children a good education, so their children wouldn’t have to do the same thing,” he said.

That economic dependence makes the changing conditions in the Himalayas particularly significant for Sherpa communities whose livelihoods are tied to mountaineering.

“While he (Tenzing Norgay) was still alive, before the 80s, nobody talked about climate change because we didn’t see the changes,” he said.

“We notice this now.”

item.title: Ronaldo hails Messi after Argentina great says he already misses national team
item.description:
Portugal captain Cristiano Ronaldo set aside one of soccer's great rivalries on Wednesday to pay tribute to Lionel Messi after the Argentine said he already missed representing his country following his emotional international retirement.

Messi delivered one final masterclass in Argentina's blue and white on Tuesday, scoring once and setting up two goals in a 3-0 friendly win over Benin before more than 85,000 fans at Buenos Aires' Monumental Stadium, where his farewell became a celebration of an extraordinary 21-year international career.

"Yesterday was my last game, and I already miss wearing the blue and white. I know I'm making the right decision," Messi said in a lengthy Instagram post. "It's been an incredible journey, full of joy and also some sadness, but I know for sure that every step I took was worth it..."

"I don't want to forget Diego (Maradona), who put our country where it deserved to be and who, as I always say, I know helped us both by being here with us and also from heaven, with every step we took."

"Thank you to the clubs where I played, for always respecting my feelings and allowing me to dedicate myself to my country whenever it was time to put on the national team jersey..."

Messi captained Argentina to the 2022 World Cup title and Copa America triumphs in 2021 and 2024, while also helping them win the 2022 Finalissima.

"I am grateful. I love you all very much; I'm going to miss you, and I will always thank you for having been by our side, by my side," the Inter Miami playmaker added.

Messi and Ronaldo have vied for recognition as the greatest player of their generation throughout their illustrious careers, with the 41-year-old Portuguese forward among those to respond to the post.

"Leo, after so many years of defending your country, you've made history that will last forever. I have the utmost respect for what you've accomplished with Argentina. A hug," Ronaldo said.

Ronaldo, meanwhile, is embroiled in a dispute with Portugal coach Jorge Jesus following his abrupt departure from the national team's training camp.

item.title: Nana Patekar dies after cardiac arrest at residence
item.description:
ANI_20260122006

Actor Nana Patekar died at 5.20 am on Thursday after suffering a cardiac arrest at his residence, Shekhar Salkar, Chief of the Department of Oncology at Manipal Hospital, told ANI over the phone.

According to Salkar, Patekar suffered cardiac arrest at his residence, and CPR was administered for 45 minutes. He remained in asystole throughout the CPR.

A medico-legal case (MLC) has been completed, while a post-mortem examination is required, according to the doctor.

The doctor confirmed Patekar’s death and said efforts to revive him continued for 45 minutes following the cardiac arrest.

Nana Patekar was one of the prominent actors in Hindi and Marathi cinema. He made his acting debut with the 1978 film ‘Gaman’ and went on to establish himself as a celebrated actor with performances in films such as ‘Parinda,’ ‘Prahar,’ ‘Angaar,’ ‘Krantiveer,’ ‘Tiranga,’ ‘Khamoshi’ and ‘Ab Tak Chhappan,’ among others.

In recent years, Patekar continued to feature in a range of projects. He was part of Housefull 5, which starred Akshay Kumar, Abhishek Bachchan, Riteish Deshmukh and others.

Patekar, 75, also appeared as a police officer in Vishal Bhardwaj’s O’Romeo, starring Shahid Kapoor and Triptii Dimri. In addition, he had a cameo appearance in Subedar, which stars Anil Kapoor and Radhika Madan.

item.title: Dhaka ranks 6th globally in air pollution
item.description:
Dhaka ranked 6th among the world's most polluted cities on Thursday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 168 at 9:10am.
The air quality was classified as "unhealthy", meaning the concentration of pollutants in the air had reached a level that could pose health risks to the general population, according to the AQI scale.
Kuala Lumpur in Malaysia ranked first with an AQI score of 225, while Lahore in Pakistan ranked second with a score of 207, followed by Kinshasa in the Democratic Republic of Congo in third place with an AQI score of 193.
According to AQI standards, a reading between 101 and 150 is considered "unhealthy for sensitive groups", while 151 to 200 is classified as "unhealthy". A reading between 201 and 300 is considered "very unhealthy", while levels above 301 are deemed "hazardous", posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides daily updates on air quality, indicating how clean or polluted the air is and highlighting potential health impacts.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution, with air quality typically deteriorating during winter and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes around seven million deaths globally each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: Bangladesh face Uzbekistan in U-17 Women's Asian Cup qualifier today
item.description:
Bangladesh will face hosts Uzbekistan in their opening Group H match of the AFC U-17 Women's Asian Cup 2027 Qualifiers at the Do'stlik Stadium Training Pitch 1 in Tashkent on Thursday.
The match will kick off at 5 pm Bangladesh time.
Ahead of the crucial opener, the Bangladesh team completed their fifth and final training session at the Uzbekistan football academy training centre (Pitch-3) on Wednesday, fine-tuning their preparations for the match.
The session focused on warm-ups, possession exercises and set-piece preparations, with the players maintaining good intensity and commitment throughout.
All players are in good health and adapting well to the local weather conditions in Tashkent.
Bangladesh head coach Saiful Bari Titu, in a video message, said the team were well prepared for their opening match against Uzbekistan.
"Definitely, getting five sessions before the first match is a good thing. We have tried our best to prepare the girls for the match. Especially, the first match is very important," he said after the team's training session.
The coach said the team's plan would be to remain calm and maintain their shape both in and out of possession, while set-pieces would also be an important part of the game.
"Overall, the girls are prepared to play the first match against Uzbekistan," he added.

item.title: Arteta targets more Arsenal glory after signing new deal until 2030
item.description:
Mikel Arteta vowed "this is only the beginning of what we can achieve together" after signing a new contract with Premier League champions Arsenal until 2030.
The Spaniard's deal had been due to expire at the end of the 2026/27 season but if he sees out his new contract he will have been at the Emirates for more than a decade.
The club said in a statement on Wednesday that the new agreement, which was widely expected, "reflects our shared belief that the progress we've made and last season's success is the beginning of a special period in our history".
Arteta has reportedly been given a substantial pay rise after leading Arsenal to their first Premier League title for 22 years following three successive runners-up finishes.
"It's a privilege to commit my future to the club and to continue to work with exceptional people who want the best for Arsenal," said the 44-year-old.
"This club is unique, its character and the way it makes you feel, and I have a great sense of privilege that our journey together will continue.
"We have already built a special bond and created memories that will last a lifetime, and what is so exciting is that this is only the beginning of what we can achieve together."
Arteta, who replaced Unai Emery in December 2019, is now the longest-serving manager in the Premier League following Pep Guardiola's departure from Manchester City.
The former Arsenal captain came under significant pressure early in his managerial reign at the Emirates but has overseen the club's return to the top of English football.
Arteta also led the Gunners to their first Champions League final in two decades last season but they lost to Paris Saint-Germain on penalties.
He has been in charge for 361 matches in all competitions, with his win percentage of just over 62 percent the best of any full-time manager in the club's history.
Arsenal are currently second in the Premier League, three points behind leaders City after a surprise 3-0 defeat to Brighton before the international break.
Club co-chairs Stan and Josh Kroenke said: "It has been an incredible journey so far and we are excited for what lies ahead in this special relationship.
"Last season was an incredible moment in Arsenal's history, a moment in which we created memories that will last a lifetime. We're determined to create many more in the years ahead.
"We share a special bond with Mikel. We are so proud of everything we have achieved since he returned to the club in 2019."
Arsenal return to Premier League action with a home match against Leeds on Saturday.

item.title: Messi’s Bangladesh: How the Argentine superstar shaped a generation
item.description:
For a generation of Bangladeshi youngsters, Lionel Messi was more than a footballer on a television screen.
He was the reason they stayed awake until the early hours to watch a match. He was the name printed on the back of their first football jersey. He was the player they tried to imitate on school grounds, alleyways and muddy village pitches.
And, for many, he was the gateway to football itself.
Bangladesh has never qualified for a FIFA World Cup, and cricket remains the country's dominant sport. Yet whenever Messi and Argentina played, the country repeatedly turned sky blue and white.
The phenomenon was not simply about supporting a foreign national team. Messi helped shape the football identity of an entire generation.
Argentina's popularity in Bangladesh did not begin with Messi.
Diego Maradona laid the foundation during the 1986 World Cup, when his extraordinary performances inspired a generation of Bangladeshis. For many older supporters, Argentina became a lifelong allegiance because of Maradona.
But Messi inherited that legacy and took it somewhere else.
Photo: AFP
Unlike Maradona, whose exploits many Bangladeshi youngsters experienced through television broadcasts and stories from their parents, Messi's career unfolded in real time on satellite television, smartphones and social media.
Young Bangladeshis could watch him every week for Barcelona, follow his goals and assists almost instantly, and discuss his performances with friends online.
That constant exposure made Messi feel less like a distant World Cup hero and more like a familiar sporting presence.
Perhaps the clearest evidence of Messi's influence can be found on Bangladesh's football pitches.
In 2022, nine-year-old Raiyan Abdulla was dubbed the country's "Mini Messi" because of his dribbling ability. He idolised the Argentine and dreamed of following in his footsteps to Barcelona.
His story was hardly unusual.
Across Bangladesh, youngsters have grown up trying to copy Messi's close control, quick changes of direction and left-footed finishing.
For children playing in cramped spaces with limited facilities, Messi's style was particularly attractive. He did not rely on physical strength. He could beat opponents through balance, intelligence, timing and technique.
A ball and a small patch of ground were enough to try to imitate him.
Messi's influence did not stop with supporters. It reached the players who eventually represented Bangladesh.
The country's national-team footballers have their own favourite clubs and players, but Argentina has traditionally had a particularly strong following among them.
Many senior and youth national-team players became ardent followers of Argentina because of Messi.
The connection is particularly striking among the women's national team.
Most Bangladesh women's national-team players have supported Argentina, with captain Sabina Khatun saying she began supporting the team in 2014 because of Messi.
Maria Manda, another key member of the national team, recalled hearing one name repeatedly while growing up in her village.
"Before 2011, when I used to stay in my village, I did not hear about Argentina but only Messi, Messi," Maria told Dhaka Tribune. "Then I started playing and watching Messi's games. I became his fan."
She admired his dribbling and ability to turn possession into goals and chances.
The influence has reached younger generations too.
Bangladesh U-20 captain Shamsunnahar has also spoken about her admiration for Messi. Asked whom she would like to meet, she immediately named the Argentine superstar and said she would ask him how he played so brilliantly.
Messi also changed what young Bangladeshi fans watched.
His dominance at Barcelona helped push European club football into the daily lives of a much wider audience. For many youngsters, supporting Argentina went hand in hand with supporting Barcelona.
Messi became their introduction to the Champions League, La Liga and elite club football.
A child who initially stayed awake to watch Argentina could soon find himself watching Barcelona against Real Madrid, learning about the Champions League and discovering players from across Europe.
Messi widened the football window.
Then came Qatar 2022.
Messi's final World Cup transformed an already enormous following into something approaching a national social phenomenon.
In Dhaka and elsewhere, thousands gathered to watch Argentina's matches. Streets and houses were decorated with sky-blue-and-white flags, giant Argentina flags appeared at rallies, and Messi's No 10 shirt became one of the most visible symbols of the tournament.
The passion stretched far beyond Dhaka, with supporters organising rallies and public screenings across the country. FIFA even shared footage of Bangladeshi fans celebrating Messi's goal against Mexico, bringing the country's extraordinary support to a global audience.
And Messi noticed.
After Argentina's World Cup triumph, he acknowledged images of Bangladeshi supporters and their affection for Argentina and his No 10 shirt.
For young Bangladeshi fans, the moment carried special significance.
The distance between Buenos Aires and Dhaka suddenly felt much smaller.
Messi's influence on Bangladesh's youngsters cannot simply be measured by the number of Argentina jerseys sold.
His greatest impact may be harder to quantify.
He made football aspirational.
For a young boy or girl playing on a school field, Messi represented the possibility that extraordinary football could come through skill and intelligence.
He showed youngsters that greatness could be built through repetition, patience and an obsessive relationship with the ball.
And his appeal crossed gender and generations.
The same player who inspired boys on neighbourhood fields also inspired Bangladesh's leading female footballers.
He did not only create fans.
He inspired footballers.
Messi's playing career is moving into its final chapter, but his influence on Bangladesh's football generation is unlikely to disappear with his retirement.
The children who copied his celebrations are growing up. The youngsters who wore No 10 shirts to school are now old enough to coach younger players. Some may eventually continue into professional football, carrying the inspiration they received from him.
For Bangladesh, Messi's greatest legacy may not be the trophies, records or Ballon d'Ors.
It may be the thousands of children who first fell in love with football because of Messi — and the national-team players who grew up watching him before eventually representing their own country.
From a muddy field in a Bangladeshi village to the biggest stadiums in the world, the same dream has travelled a remarkably long distance.
For many of them, it began with a ball, a television screen and one name: Messi.

Bangladesh, 3 other South Asian countries launch new initiative to tackle extreme heat
item.description:
The El Niño phenomenon is strengthening across the Pacific, increasing the risk of another season of extreme heat in South Asia.

Against this backdrop, India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Bhutan have launched a joint initiative to tackle the impacts of extreme heat.

Four new country briefs assessing heatwave conditions, preparedness and gaps in the four countries were released today, Thursday, at the Global Heat Forum, which began in Bangkok, the capital of Thailand, says a press release.

The briefs were published under the initiative of the South Asia Hub of the Global Heat Health Information Network (GHHIN). The assessments were conducted as part of a review of countries’ preparedness and capacity as health risks from extreme heat continue to rise across South Asia. They examine how the countries are responding to extreme heat, preparing in advance and where significant gaps remain.

The Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW) in New Delhi runs the South Asia Hub. Its partners include the Sustainable Futures Collaborative, Natural Resources Defense Council, BRAC James P Grant School of Public Health, and the UN Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UNESCAP). The initiative is also aligned with the joint climate and health programme of the World Health Organisation (WHO) and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).

Heatwaves in South Asia have become more intense and longer in recent years. Extreme heat causes more than discomfort; it poses serious health risks, particularly for children, older people, pregnant women and outdoor workers. In addition to heat-related illness and deaths, extreme heat can increase the risks of heart disease, respiratory illnesses and other health problems.

The purpose of the new assessments of the four countries is to identify areas where progress has been made in addressing heat-related health risks and where more coordinated action is needed. The findings could be used in policymaking, strengthening health systems, early warning systems and protecting vulnerable populations.

The Global Heat Forum in Bangkok is discussing the growing risk of extreme heat and its health impacts in South Asia and other regions around the world. Experts have warned that climate change could further increase the risk of heatwaves in the future. As a result, there is growing emphasis on treating heat not simply as a weather event but as a major public health risk.

In Bangladesh, the feels-like temperature, which takes both temperature and humidity into account, has risen by about 4.5°C since 1980. People now spend nearly one-third of the year in dangerously humid heat.

Heat has been recognised as a risk in Bangladesh’s National Adaptation Plan. The country’s first urban heatwave action plan has been developed for Narayanganj. National guidelines for dealing with heat-related illness and a public awareness campaign called “Beat the Heat” have also been launched.

Despite these initiatives, however, there is a lack of dedicated heatwave action plans at both national and local levels. It is also important to establish a system for monitoring heat-related illness by linking weather forecasts with hospitals and the health system.

These findings and recommendations are included in the first Bangladesh assessment by the South Asia Hub of the Global Heat Health Information Network (GHHIN). Four separate assessments of heat and health conditions in Bangladesh, India, Nepal and Bhutan were released today, Thursday, at the Global Heat Forum in Bangkok, Thailand.

First assessments of the four countries

This is the first assessment by the GHHIN South Asia Hub of heat and health risks in the four countries.

At the time of the release, it was announced that El Niño is strengthening in the Pacific, which could increase the risk of another season of extreme heat in South Asia. Against this backdrop, Bangladesh, India, Nepal and Bhutan have begun working together to address the impacts of extreme heat.

Plans have advanced, but implementation remains a challenge

The assessment of the four countries says preparations for tackling heat in South Asia have progressed most rapidly in the areas of planning, weather forecasting and early warning. All four countries have developed heatwave action plans and early warning systems in one form or another.

However, measures to translate these plans and warnings into protection on the ground have not advanced at the same pace. Major gaps remain in monitoring heat-related illness, financing local-level initiatives, and integrating heat risks into health, labour and urban planning. While several countries have begun large-scale initiatives, progress is uneven.

Extreme heat was once mainly seen in the plains of South Asia. It is now spreading to the Himalayan countries of Nepal and Bhutan as well.

Health risks in Bangladesh remain under-recognised

Farzana Misha of the BRAC James P Grant School of Public Health said, “Heat is one of the least recognised health risks in this region. It is less visible than floods or cyclones. But its impacts on health, work and food security are no less serious. In Bangladesh, we have already started taking some initiatives. A national guideline for dealing with heat-related illness and the country’s first urban heatwave action plan in Narayanganj have been developed. Similar initiatives are being undertaken in Dhaka, Rajshahi and other urban centres. Now similar action is needed across South Asia. We need to build health systems and provide the necessary financing so that risks can be identified before the heat arrives and action can be taken before people are affected.”

The Bangladesh assessment recommends developing dedicated heatwave action plans at both national and local levels. It also calls for establishing a system to monitor heat and health by linking the country’s weather forecasts with hospitals.

India has made the most progress

Among the four countries, India has made the most progress in shifting from reactive relief measures to anticipatory action to reduce heat risks.
District-level research by CEEW found that 57 per cent of India’s districts are at high or very high risk of extreme heat. Nearly three-quarters of the country’s population live in these districts.

More than 250 heatwave action plans are in place at the city and district levels in India. Heatwaves have also been officially recognised as a natural disaster under the country’s disaster risk management financing framework. A national system for monitoring heat-related illness has been established, and more than 18,000 medical officers have been trained.
However, the assessment recommends taking India’s heat action plans beyond the boundaries of disaster management. It calls for dedicated financing and systems to assess health outcomes to be included in every plan.

Nepal experienced 50 days of temperatures above 40°C

Nepal, a Himalayan country, has traditionally faced floods, droughts and other water- and weather-related disasters. It is now also facing the risk of extreme heat.

According to data from Nepal’s national meteorological department, temperatures in the country’s southern Terai plains exceeded 40°C for 50 days in 2024.

Nepal has already published its first national heatwave action plan and issues risk-based warnings. However, the country’s health system does not yet routinely record data on heat-related illness.

The assessment recommends making it mandatory for hospitals in the Terai region to record admissions related to extreme heat. It also calls for strengthening the process of ensuring that weather warnings reach local communities and that appropriate action is taken accordingly.

Heat is rising even in Bhutan’s cooler valleys

Bhutan’s southern lowlands are becoming warmer. As a result, temperatures are also rising in valleys that were previously cooler. Communities that had never before needed to plan for extreme heat are now at risk.

Bhutan’s national policy assigns responsibility for tackling heat to the Ministry of Health. A 2022 regulation also requires measures to protect workers from heat.

Bhutan has relatively advanced early warning systems for floods and glacial lake outburst disasters. The assessment says these systems could also be expanded to cover heat. It recommends bringing different policies and responsibilities together to develop an integrated national heatwave action plan.

Forecasts must be turned into protection

Biswas Chitale, a fellow at CEEW and chair of the GHHIN South Asia Hub, said extreme heat is now a year-round regional risk in South Asia.

However, the region does not have to start from scratch in tackling the risk. Every country is projected to experience worse heat conditions than five years ago.

According to Chitale, the key task now is to link weather forecasts with health systems, local budgets and labour regulations. A warning must be turned into effective protection for people.

Kyeong Ko, director of the Information and Communication Technology and Disaster Risk Reduction Division at UNESCAP, said heat does not stop at borders. Therefore, responses to it should not be confined within national borders either. Countries can share forecasts, coordinate temperature thresholds for taking action and incorporate heat risks into existing disaster management systems.

Following the Global Heat Forum, the South Asia Hub will develop a regional network and training programme involving various organisations. Situation assessments will also be prepared for the governments of the four countries before and after the heat season. The goal will be to turn scientific information on heat into coordinated action and ensure the protection of the region’s most vulnerable populations.

item.title: DP World deal raises question of whether BNP came to power by signing an undertaking: Odhikar Committee
item.description:
Opposing the agreement with UAE-based company DP World to operate Chittagong port’s New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT), the Gonotantrik Odhikar Committee (Democratic Rights Committee) said there had been no discussion in parliament on the US trade agreement.

The committee said that, ignoring concerns over threats to the country’s sovereignty, the signing of the agreement with DP World has raised questions in people’s minds about whether the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) had come to power by signing an undertaking to an imperialist country.

The Gonotantrik Odhikar Committee made the statement in a press release sent to the media on Thursday afternoon. A 15-year concession agreement for Chittagong port was signed with DP World at the Invest Bangladesh office (formerly BIDA) in Agargaon, Dhaka, on Thursday afternoon.

CPA, DP World sign deal to boost Chittagong port capacity

Police baton-charged a protest organised there by various left-wing parties and organisations, including the CPB and Basad. The committee strongly condemned the attack in its statement.

According to the Gonotantrik Odhikar Committee’s statement, the previous Awami League government and the interim government had also taken initiatives to hand over Chittagong port’s New Mooring Container Terminal to foreign company DP World, despite the terminal being profitable under local operators.

However, the governments backed down in the face of protests by left-wing and democratic forces in the country. The BNP government, which subsequently came to power after winning the election, signed the agreement today, ignoring all opposition.

During the signing of the agreement today, several people were injured when police attacked protesters outside the venue. They included Gonotantrik Odhikar Committee member Seema Dutta, CPB President Kazi Sazzad Zahir Chandan, party leader Moniruzzaman Milon, Basad central committee member Monisha Chakraborty and Bangladesh Chhatra Union leader Asif Zaman, among others.

NCT handover to DP World sparks protest in capital, police baton-charge

Alleging that the government has already yielded to pressure from imperialist countries, the Gonotantrik Odhikar Committee said that the failure to discuss the US trade agreement in parliament, the purchase of Boeing aircraft from the United States, the purchase of Airbus aircraft from France, and the signing of the DP World agreement while ignoring the demands of port workers and concerns over threats to the country’s sovereignty has raised questions in people’s minds about whether the BNP had come to power by signing undertakings to these imperialist countries.

It said no such example had been seen before of a government, within six months of coming to power, openly protecting the interests of imperialist countries while ignoring the national interest.

Regarding the role of the current opposition parties, the Gonotantrik Odhikar Committee said, “Those who are in the opposition today and hope to come to power in the future also agree with the government on this issue. These so-called major parties have no stance on the matter, either inside or outside parliament.”

Chittagong Port: DP World seeks CCT alongside NCT

The Gonotantrik Odhikar Committee said handing over the country’s principal seaport, which handles the bulk of its foreign trade, to foreigners posed risks to national security, economic independence and sovereignty. It said handing over important national infrastructure or “strategic assets” to profit-driven groups or foreign interests was a self-destructive decision for the country. The government would be held responsible for the dire consequences in the future, it said.

Chhatra Union calls for cancellation of deal

Meanwhile, Bangladesh Chhatra Union has issued a statement demanding cancellation of the agreement with DP World over the New Mooring Terminal.

In a joint statement on Thursday, a faction’s central president Mahir Shahriar and general secretary Bahauddin Shuvo said, “We urge the government to remember the fate of the then BNP government following the 2006 Phulbari mass movement and cancel all decisions that go against the interests of the country. If the government does not heed this demand of the people, it will be forced to accept the demand through a strong movement.”

item.title: Primary teacher: Clinton ranks second, but receives no appointment letter
item.description:
“I am a Bangladeshi citizen and have a national identity (NID) card. I did not get the job simply because I do not have a permanent address. Yet I ranked second on the merit list. My merit was not taken into consideration; instead, I was denied an appointment letter solely because I do not have a permanent address. I applied to be given the job on humanitarian grounds, but the authorities did not accept my application,” said Clinton Saha, who lives in the Choumuhani area of Chattogram city

Clinton Saha passed both the written and viva voce examinations for the recruitment of assistant teachers at government primary schools and ranked second in the thana-based merit list.

He was also recommended for appointment. However, he was not appointed because of complications regarding his permanent address during the final verification.

Clinton Saha said his family had long been victims of river erosion and displacement. Their homes and shops had been washed away by river erosion about seven times. The house they later owned was also sold many years ago. As a result, they have been living in the city for about 21 years. They currently do not have their own permanent homestead.

Last Tuesday, Clinton Saha went to the office of the Chattogram district primary education officer to submit an application. However, as the district primary education officer was not at the office that day, his application was not accepted.

He said over the phone that he had requested an official at the office to accept the application, but the official was unwilling to do so.

According to sources at the Chattogram District Primary Education Office, the recruitment list published in March this year contained the names of 12 people for the Double Mooring Education Thana.

Clinton's name was 10th on the list. The number ‘2’ was written in the merit-ranking column beside his name. At the time, five people were given appointment letters. Six more were given appointment letters in September. Clinton was the only one who did not receive an appointment letter.

Everything was lost to river erosion

Clinton Saha's ancestral home is in Hatia upazila of Noakhali. His father had a business and shop there. Their permanent address was also there. However, when Clinton was very young, they had to move to Chattogram in 2005 because of river erosion. Their home was washed away by the river about seven times. After moving to Chattogram, his father started a retail business selling vegetables and fruits.

Clinton said he is the youngest of three sisters and one brother. His two elder sisters are married. His younger sister has also completed higher education. At present, he lives with his parents and one sister as members of the same family. As his father is elderly and ill, he has to bear a large portion of the family's expenses. He supported his own education by tutoring.

After moving to Chattogram in 2005, Clinton Saha's family rented a house in the Moghaltuli area under Double Mooring police station in the city.

He grew up there. In 2014, he passed his Secondary School Certificate examination from Pathantuli City Corporation Boys' High School and later passed higher secondary from Dewanhat City Corporation College.

He completed his bachelor's and master's degrees in physics from Chattogram College.

Clinton Saha said, “During the verification, I explained that we had a house before, but it was washed away by river erosion. I also showed the deeds of the land that we had. Later, I provided the address of my maternal grandfather's house in Sandwip. But during the next round of verification, I was again asked about my permanent address. I explained the same thing then as well. Even after that, I was not given the job.”

Saying that he has lost interest in sitting for job examinations, Clinton Saha said, “I am now afraid of sitting for any job examination. I feel that even if I pass the written examination, what will I say if they ask about my permanent address during the viva? This is why I no longer feel interested in taking any examination. I am currently mentally devastated.”

‘We cannot disclose the reason; it is confidential’

According to sources at the district primary education office, 24 people were dropped from a list of 551 candidates for the recruitment of assistant teachers at government primary schools because they did not submit the required documents. Appointment letters were issued to 525 of the remaining 527 candidates. However, the education office did not disclose why it was unable to issue appointment letters to two people. One of them is Clinton Saha.

District Primary Education Officer Firoz Ahmed said, “We are not authorised to disclose the reason. It is confidential. We have issued the appointment letters according to the instructions given to us. Twenty-four people did not submit the documents. And appointment letters were not issued to two people. There is actually nothing more to say beyond this.”

However, talking to officials at the primary education office revealed that some candidates had been dropped from the primary assistant teacher recruitment process because of political affiliations and complications regarding permanent addresses. It is not clear exactly why Clinton Saha was dropped. However, there are complications regarding his permanent address. This is one of the reasons.

Deputy commissioner heads the district posting committee responsible for the recruitment and posting process of assistant teachers at government primary schools.

Asked about the matter, Chattogram Deputy Commissioner Mohammad Zahidul Islam Mia said no one had yet submitted such an application to the district administration. If an application is submitted, it will be sent to the ministry.

item.title: BRAC offers Tk 5,000 monthly scholarship for college students
item.description:
Applications are now open for BRAC’s Medhabikash Scholarship. Students newly admitted to colleges in the 2026–27 academic year can apply for the scholarship. Selected students will receive a one-time grant of Tk 8,000 and a monthly stipend of Tk 5,000. The deadline for applications is 21 October 2026.

According to a BRAC notice on the Medhabikash Scholarship, the programme provides scholarships funded by BRAC to help financially disadvantaged but meritorious students pursue their higher education.

Eligibility

Applicants must have been selected for admission to a government or private college for the 2026–27 academic year.

The applicant’s family must have a monthly income of Tk 20,000 or less.

Scholarship amount

Each selected student will receive a one-time scholarship of Tk 8,000 from BRAC. They will also receive a monthly stipend of Tk 5,000.

Selection criteria

a. The student must have obtained a GPA of 5 in the SSC or equivalent examination.

b. The student must come from a financially disadvantaged family.

c. The student must have been selected for admission to a government or private college.

d. Preference will be given to children of members enrolled in BRAC programmes.

e. BRAC graduates and students from disadvantaged groups, such as persons with disabilities and Indigenous students, will be given preference. In such cases, the academic result requirement may be relaxed.

Special instructions for applicants

Academic year/session: The scholarship is only for students who have newly enrolled in a government or private college in the 2026–27 academic year (Session: 2026–27).

Providing accurate information: Applicants must carefully complete every section of the application. In particular, they must ensure that the SSC GPA and college admission information are provided correctly.

Document scanning: Clear scanned copies of all required original certificates, mark sheets and proof of college admission must be uploaded in PDF or JPEG format. Blurry or unclear images will render the application ineligible.

Family income details: Applicants must provide accurate information about their family’s monthly or annual income. Supporting documents may be verified at a later stage, if necessary.

Contact information: The mobile number and email address provided in the form must remain active so that the applicant can be contacted later if necessary.

Warning: Providing incorrect or incomplete information will result in the application being cancelled at any stage.

Apply here

For more information about the scholarship, visit the relevant BRAC page.
